And a sign of his mind is, first, that he set apart for Constantius this portion which he had supposed earlier should belong to himself; then that, ending his life, leaving the eldest and the youngest at leisure, he called this one, who was busy, and entrusted to him all the affairs of the empire. And having become master of all, he dealt with his brothers so justly and so temperately, that they, neither called nor coming to one another, fell into faction and fought, while toward him they were neither angry nor blaming. And when their faction had an unfortunate end, though it was possible for him to lay claim to more, he willingly gave it up, supposing that the same virtue is needed for many nations and for few, but that greater cares, I think, lie about whoever must tend and care for more. For he does not suppose kingship to be a means of luxury, nor that, as in the case of money, those who waste it on drink and pleasures contrive an abundance of greater revenues, so the king ought to provide himself, nor to take up a war, except for the benefit of the ruled. So, conceding to the other the larger share, while himself with virtue having the less, he supposed that he had the advantage by the better. And that it was not through fear rather than through his preparation that he loved quiet, let the war that fell out afterward be a plain proof to you. He used his arms, at any rate, against that man's forces afterward in his own defence. And here again, those men admire the conquering; but I far more the taking up the war with justice, and the bearing it through courageously and very skilfully, and, when fortune put the end to it, the using the victory dexterously, temperately and royally, and altogether the showing oneself worthy of conquering.

Will you, then, that of these things too we call the witnesses by name, as in the courts? That no war was ever waged before, neither by the Greeks against Troy nor by the Macedonians against the Persians—which indeed seem to have been just—on so great a ground, is plain even to a child; for those took a very fresh vengeance for very ancient wrongs, falling neither on the children nor on the descendants, but on him who had robbed and deprived the descendants of the wrongdoers of their rule. And Agamemnon was set on avenging "the strivings and groans for Helen's sake," and marched against the Trojans wishing to avenge a single woman. But for the emperor the wrongs were still fresh, and his rule was not like Darius' or Priam's—a noble man deemed worthy of the kingship belonging to him perhaps through virtue or by birth—but a shameless and rough barbarian of those captured not long before. And what he did and how he ruled, it is neither pleasant for me to tell nor in season; but that the emperor warred against him in justice, you have heard. Of his experience and courage the signs before mentioned are enough; but more trustworthy, I think, are the deeds than the words.

As for what happened upon the victory, and how there was no further need of the sword, not even if anyone was under suspicion of greater crimes, nor if anyone had become a closer friend to the tyrant, nor indeed if anyone, gratifying him, had deemed it right to bear his herald's staff and reviled the emperor, did he pay the penalty for his rashness—unless he was base in other respects—consider, by Zeus the god of friendship. What kind of thing is reviling? How truly heart-biting and tearing the soul more than iron the skin! For it provoked even Odysseus to defend himself as he could by word and deed; he quarrelled, at least, over it with his host, though himself a wanderer and a stranger, and that too knowing that
"Foolish . . . and worthless is the man Who offers grievous strife to his host";

and Alexander the son of Philip, and Achilles the son of Thetis, and certain others not base nor ignoble men. But it belonged, I think, only to Socrates and a few rare emulators of his, who became truly happy and blessed, to strip off the last tunic of ambition. For ambition is a terribly ambitious passion, and seems for this reason rather to be implanted in noble souls; for they are vexed at reviling as most contrary to themselves, and they hate those who cast such words at them more than those who bring the iron and plot murder, and suppose them their enemies by nature and not by convention, since the one party loves praise and honour, while the other not only takes these away but contrives false slanders besides. Of this passion they say even Heracles and certain others were not masters. But I neither believe the story about those men, and I have seen the emperor very self-controlledly turn aside reviling—a deed no meaner, as I judge, than taking Troy and routing a noble phalanx. And if anyone disbelieves and thinks it neither great nor worthy of so much praise, let him judge, looking to himself, when he falls into such a misfortune; and to him we shall not seem to talk much nonsense, as I am persuaded.

Being such and having become so, the emperor after the war is reasonably not only longed for and beloved by his friends—sharing with many honour and power and freedom of speech, and bestowing on them abundant money and allowing them to use their wealth as each wishes—but he seemed such even to his enemies. And let this too be a manifest proof to you: men of the senate, all that was of worth, surpassing the rest in dignity and wealth and understanding, fleeing as into a harbour to his right hand, leaving hearths and houses and children, embraced Paeonia instead of Rome, and his company instead of their dearest; and a squadron of chosen horsemen with their standards, leading their general, deemed it right to share with him the danger rather than with the other the good fortune. And all this was done before the battle which the earlier discourse set on the banks of the Draos; for from then they were already firmly confident, while before that the tyrants' affairs seemed to prevail, some advantage having been gained over the emperor's scouts, which made him senseless with pleasure and threw into confusion those who could not reach nor see through the generalship. But he was undismayed and noble, like a good ship's pilot when a squall has suddenly burst from the clouds, and then upon it the god shakes the deep and the shores. For there the inexperienced were seized by a strange and dreadful fear, while he already rejoices and is glad, hoping for an exact calm and stillness of wind. For it is said that Poseidon, when he shakes the earth, stills the waves. And fortune deceives the senseless and trips them in greater things, allowing them small advantages, while to the prudent she grants firm confidence about the greater things, whenever she troubles them in the lesser. This the Lacedaemonians suffered at the Pass, yet did not give up nor fear the Mede advancing upon them, though they had given up three hundred Spartans and their king at the entrances of Greece; this the Romans, having often suffered it, afterward set right with greater deeds; which the emperor too, considering and reckoning, in no way failed of his judgment.

But since the discourse has once willingly come to this and recounts the goodwill of the multitude and of those in office and of the guards—who indeed help him guard the empire and ward off the enemy—will you that I tell you a manifest proof of it, which happened yesterday, as it were, or the day before? A man of those set over the armies in Gaul—perhaps you know both his name and his character—left as a hostage of friendship and faith his son to the emperor, who needed nothing of the kind; then he was more faithless than the lions, with whom, it is said, there are no trusty oaths toward men, snatching the money from the cities and distributing it to the barbarians who came on, and as it were paying it down as ransom, though he might have furnished his safety by the sword and not by money; but he sought to bring them over to goodwill through money. And at last, taking up from the women's quarters a purple robe, he appeared a truly laughable tyrant and in truth a thing of tragedy. Then the soldiers were grieved at his faithlessness, and not enduring to see the wretch clad in a woman's garb, setting upon him they tore him in pieces, not bearing that the moon's orb should rule over them. This honour, then, the emperor had from the goodwill of his guards—a wonderful return for a blameless and just rule. And what manner of man he was upon it you long to hear; but this too has not escaped you—that he chose to be neither harsh toward that man's son nor suspicious and dreadful toward his friends, but was as gentle as possible and kindly to all, though many wished to play the informer and had their goads lifted against the guiltless. And though perhaps many were truly liable to the suspicions about them, he was alike gentle to all who were not convicted nor shown to be partners of the strange and accursed counsels. But the keeping of faith and oaths toward the son of him who broke the law and trampled it—shall we truly call it kingly and divine, or shall we rather approve Agamemnon, harsh and bitter against the Trojans, not only against those who went out with Paris and outraged the hearth of Menelaus, but even against those yet unborn, and whose mothers perhaps had not yet been born when he conceived the plan of the rape? If, then, one thinks the savage and rough and inhuman least befits a king, but the gentle and kind and humane befits one who least rejoices in punishments and is grieved at the misfortunes of his subjects, however they come about—whether through their own baseness and ignorance, or brought on from without by fortune—he plainly gives the prize to the emperor.

For consider how, toward the son, he proved better and juster than the one who begot him, and toward that man's friends more faithful than the one who professed friendship. For the one gave them all up, the other saved them all. And if that man, knowing this about the emperor's character, having understood it over a long time, strongly trusted that his son's affairs lay safe with him and his friends' affairs rode at firm anchor, he understood rightly, but was often a knave and base and unhappy, wishing to be the enemy of such a man, and hating and plotting against and robbing of what he ought not, one whom he knew to be exceedingly good and especially gentle. But if, while his son's safety found him beyond hope, and his friends' and kinsmen's safety hard and impossible, he nonetheless chose faithlessness, then he was for these reasons too base and senseless and more savage than the beasts, while the other was tame and gentle and great-souled—pitying the infant's age and character, gentle toward those not convicted, and overlooking and despising the villainies. For he who concedes things which not even one of his enemies, through the greatness of the wrongs he is conscious of, hopes for, is reasonably the bearer of the prize of virtue—transferring justice to the better and gentler side, surpassing in temperance those who set a measure to punishments, excelling in courage by supposing no enemy worth reckoning, and showing wisdom by joining in the dissolution of enmities and not passing them on to children or descendants, on the pretext of exact justice and of wishing, very reasonably as it were, to make away with the seed of the wicked like a pine. For this deed indeed belongs to them, and upon it an ancient saying set the image. But the good king, imitating exactly the god, knows that even from rocks swarms of bees fly out, and from the bitterest wood the sweet fruit grows—I mean the graceful figs—and from thorns the pomegranate, and other things grow from others unlike those that beget and bear them. So he does not think these ought to be destroyed before their prime, but to await the time and permit them, having thrust off their fathers' folly and madness, to become good and temperate; while those who become emulators of their fathers' practices will undergo justice in due season, not consumed beforehand for the deeds and misfortunes of others.

Do we seem to you, then, to have sufficiently completed the true praise? Or do you long to hear also of his endurance and his gravity, and how he is not only unconquered by his enemies, but was never taken by base desire, nor, desiring a fine house or a costly country-seat or necklaces of emeralds, took them by force or even by persuasion from those who possessed them; nor any free woman nor handmaid, nor altogether loved unjust love; and how he does not demand the measureless surfeit even of the good things the seasons bring forth, nor cares for ice in summertime, nor changes his dwelling with the seasons, but is ever present to the toiling parts of his empire, holding out nobly both against the cold and against the heat? If you bid me bring you the manifest proofs of these things, I will tell of things known and shall not be at a loss; but the discourse would be long and far-resounding, and I have no leisure to serve the Muses so far, but it is now time to turn to the work.
